title: Financial Statement Analysis & Adjustments
description: Review how accounting adjustments affect assets, liabilities, income, equity, and key financial statement relationships.
html:
The FAR Big Picture

FAR questions often require more than knowing an isolated accounting rule.

You may need to determine how an adjustment affects several financial statement accounts at the same time.

ACCOUNTING EVENT ↓ RECOGNITION ↓ MEASUREMENT ↓ FINANCIAL STATEMENT EFFECT

Start With the Accounting Equation

ASSETS = LIABILITIES + EQUITY

Every adjustment must preserve the accounting equation.

Example — Accrued Expense

A company owes employees $12,000 of salaries at year-end that have not yet been recorded.

Salary Expense + $12,000
Salaries Payable + $12,000
Net Income − $12,000
Equity − $12,000

Example — Accrued Revenue

A company has earned $8,000 of service revenue but has not yet billed the customer.

Receivable + $8,000
Revenue + $8,000
Net Income + $8,000
Equity + $8,000

Unearned Revenue

Cash received before the related performance obligation is satisfied generally creates a liability.

CASH RECEIVED FIRST → LIABILITY PERFORMANCE LATER → REDUCE LIABILITY + RECOGNIZE REVENUE

Example — Advance Collection

A company receives $24,000 for twelve months of services beginning immediately.

After three months:

$24,000 ÷ 12 = $2,000 PER MONTH $2,000 × 3 = $6,000 REVENUE EARNED $24,000 − $6,000 = $18,000 LIABILITY REMAINING

Prepaid Expenses

A prepaid cost initially represents an asset. As the benefit is consumed, the asset decreases and expense is recognized.

PREPAYMENT → ASSET BENEFIT CONSUMED → EXPENSE

Depreciation Adjustment

Depreciation allocates the depreciable cost of a long-lived asset over its useful life.

STRAIGHT-LINE DEPRECIATION = COST − RESIDUAL VALUE ÷ USEFUL LIFE
Example

Equipment cost: $110,000

Residual value: $10,000

Useful life: 5 years

($110,000 − $10,000) ÷ 5 = $20,000 ANNUAL DEPRECIATION
Depreciation Expense + $20,000
Accumulated Depreciation + $20,000
Net Income − $20,000
Carrying Amount of Assets − $20,000

Allowance for Credit Losses

Receivables should reflect the amount expected to be collected.

GROSS RECEIVABLE − ALLOWANCE FOR CREDIT LOSSES = NET RECEIVABLE

Accounts receivable: $300,000

Required allowance: $18,000

$300,000 − $18,000 = $282,000 NET RECEIVABLE

Inventory Errors

Inventory errors can affect both the balance sheet and income statement.

COGS = BEGINNING INVENTORY + PURCHASES − ENDING INVENTORY

If ending inventory is overstated:

Ending Inventory Overstated
COGS Understated
Net Income Overstated
Assets Overstated

Current Ratio

CURRENT RATIO = CURRENT ASSETS ÷ CURRENT LIABILITIES

Current assets: $450,000

Current liabilities: $300,000

$450,000 ÷ $300,000 = 1.50

Working Capital

WORKING CAPITAL = CURRENT ASSETS − CURRENT LIABILITIES
$450,000 − $300,000 = $150,000

FAR Adjustment Strategy

1. IDENTIFY THE EVENT 2. IDENTIFY ACCOUNTS AFFECTED 3. DETERMINE DEBIT / CREDIT EFFECT 4. CALCULATE THE ADJUSTMENT 5. FOLLOW THE EFFECT TO NET INCOME AND EQUITY 6. RECHECK THE ACCOUNTING EQUATION

Common CPA Trap

Do not focus only on the account directly mentioned in the question.

An adjustment to one account may affect assets, liabilities, revenue or expense, net income, and equity simultaneously.

Key Takeaways

  • Every adjustment must preserve the accounting equation.
  • Accrued expenses increase liabilities and decrease income.
  • Accrued revenues increase assets and income.
  • Advance collections generally remain liabilities until revenue is earned.
  • Ending inventory errors affect both COGS and net income.
  • Always trace an adjustment through the financial statements.

quiz.prompt: A company fails to record $15,000 of salaries incurred but unpaid at year-end. Before correction, which combination is correct?

choices.text: Liabilities are overstated and net income is understated
Assets are understated and net income is overstated
Liabilities are understated and net income is overstated
Liabilities are understated and net income is understated

quiz.explanation: Failing to accrue the salaries omits both salary expense and salaries payable. Therefore, liabilities are understated by $15,000 and expenses are understated, causing net income to be overstated by $15,000.

objectives: Explain financial statement analysis & adjustments and its underlying principles.
Apply the topic to a financial-reporting scenario.
Evaluate common errors and their financial-statement effects.
